shots.narration: Hunters call this animal the Black Death.
It eats grass, and a bull can outweigh a small car.
Later, Doug faces a thousand buffalo beside a lion, and the lion runs.
The Dagga Boy.
Safari guides will tell you that the buffalo to worry about is not the big herd,
but the lone old bull lying in the mud.
Guides call these bulls dagga boys, a name that comes from udaka, the Zulu word for mud,
because they spend the hot part of the day lying in wallows.
Old bulls are often seen caked in a crust of dried mud.
The nickname Black Death comes from hunting stories, not from any measured ranking of dangerous animals.
But the stories keep pointing at the same kind of buffalo.
Here's the strange part.
The Black Death is mostly retired,
because at around twelve years old, most bulls move away from the breeding herd and the safety that comes with it.
They live alone, or in small bachelor groups of other old males,
usually somewhere close to water and mud.
Picture the retired neighbour who shouts at anyone who walks too close to his lawn.
Now give him horns, a bad back, and the weight of a small car.
Doug signed up for a photo safari.
Doug did not agree to this.
He crept right to the edge of the mud for a close-up,
because the light was perfect and the bull looked asleep.
Doug deaths: three hundred and ninety-seven.
The photo came out blurry, and that bull is not finished with this episode yet.
One.
The Boss.
A mature buffalo bull wears a helmet across his forehead, and he grew it himself.
As a young bull gets older, the bases of his horns thicken and spread
until they meet in the middle of his head.
The result is one continuous shield over the top of the skull, solid bone covered in horn, and it is called the boss.
On a big bull, the tips of the horns can be more than a metre apart.
A big bull can weigh more than eight hundred kilograms.
That is heavier than a small two-seat city car,
if the car were wearing a crash helmet and had opinions.
But that's not the interesting part.
The helmet takes years to finish.
A bull's horns are fully grown by about five or six,
but the boss does not become hard until he is around eight or nine years old.
So the pensioner from a minute ago is the one wearing the finished version.
Doug saw the boss coming and went straight up the nearest tree.
The bull lay down underneath it and began to chew,
with no plans to be anywhere else.
Doug is fine.
Doug has a new address, and it is a branch.
On the third day the bull wandered off,
and it turned out he had been carrying passengers the whole time.
The Hitchhikers.
The birds riding around on a buffalo's back may not be working for the buffalo at all.
They are oxpeckers, red-billed and yellow-billed,
and they clamber over large African mammals picking off ticks and other parasites.
In one study in Kruger, yellow-billed oxpeckers were only ever seen feeding on Cape buffalo.
From a distance, it looks like a very good cleaning service.
The worst part is the menu.
Oxpeckers also eat earwax, dead skin and wound tissue,
and they are known to drink blood.
When a scientist kept the birds away from cattle in Zimbabwe,
the tick numbers did not change,
but the wounds on those cattle healed faster without them.
In the wild, the picture is less clear,
because the Kruger study saw wound feeding only six times in eight hundred and fifty-five observations.
But the birds are always there, and the buffalo lets them stay.
Imagine hiring a cleaner who tidies the whole house
and then, now and then, has a little sip of you.
Doug lay down in the grass to blend in with the herd.
An oxpecker landed on him,
checked him from his boots to his cap,
found no ticks, and flew away.
Doug is fine.
Doug was not worth the landing, which was honestly a disappointment.
The bird went back to its buffalo, and the buffalo walked into the reeds to get out of the sun.
The Thicket.
In the heat of the day, a buffalo you cannot see may be lying a few steps away from you.
Buffalo look for refuge from heat and danger in woodland, thickets and reed beds.
In one Kruger study, herds rested more by day and fed more at night when the weather was hotter.
A grown bull can settle into the cover and simply vanish.
The reeds are taller than Doug
and about as dense as the spinning brushes in a car wash.
Once you are inside, you can see roughly one arm's length ahead,
and a buffalo lying still is just one more dark shape among the stems.
Old hunting stories go further than that.
They claim a buffalo will loop back along its own tracks
and lie quietly in the thick cover, waiting for whoever is following it.
Here's the problem.
Nobody has ever measured that,
and there is no study showing a buffalo planning an ambush or holding a grudge against anyone.
What guides do agree on is much simpler:
the lone old bulls are the ones to watch, and reeds hide them extremely well.
Doug found a line of fresh tracks leading into the reeds,
and he followed them, for the light.
Then the reeds stopped moving.
Doug deaths: three hundred and ninety-eight, from a single buffalo, and most buffalo do not live alone.
The herd.
The Vote.
A buffalo herd decides where to go next by holding a vote,
and mostly only the adult cows take part.
The ecologist Herbert Prins watched a herd of almost a thousand buffalo at Lake Manyara in Tanzania.
In the hour before the evening feed, cows would stand up one at a time,
stare in a single direction for about a minute,
and then lie back down.
Then the whole herd would rise together
and walk off in the average direction of all those stares.
The bulls and the young animals mostly stayed out of it,
and a review in the journal Nature later described this as voting.
Here's the uncomfortable part.
It is a meeting where everybody votes by pointing,
and afterwards the meeting walks straight over you.
Doug stood up in the middle of the resting herd and cast his vote in the opposite direction.
Every cow in the herd had voted the other way,
and nobody called a second vote on whether to walk around him.
The herd left in the direction it had chosen,
and Doug was standing in that direction.
Doug deaths: three hundred and ninety-nine.
The herd never noticed, and its next weapon does not need to touch anyone.
The Carrier.
Botswana has built more than ten thousand kilometres of fences,
and a big reason is the buffalo.
That is about a quarter of the way around the planet.
Some of those fences, like the Southern Buffalo Fence finished in nineteen eighty-two,
went up mainly to keep buffalo in the wild areas and away from the cattle farms.
Buffalo carry the virus behind foot-and-mouth disease,
and infected buffalo show few or no signs of being ill,
while the cattle on the other side of the fence are not so lucky.
But that's not the only thing they carry.
A tick can pick up a tiny parasite from a buffalo and pass it on to cattle.
In cattle, the result is Corridor disease,
which kills about eight in every ten animals that get it,
while in buffalo the same parasite is usually harmless.
It is named after its first South African outbreak, in a corridor between two game reserves in KwaZulu-Natal.
The buffalo's most expensive weapon never touches anyone.
It just stands there, chewing.
Corridor disease is a cattle disease, which is exactly why Doug is dressed as a cow.
He grazed politely beside the herd for one afternoon,
and a tick found him.
Doug deaths: four hundred,
and the herd has not even started defending itself yet.
The Bodyguards.
Buffalo come back for each other,
and a herd under attack can stop being the prey and start being the problem.
When lions get too close, a herd bunches together, turns to face them
and chases them away.
And if lions do manage to catch one, other members of the herd may come back to drive the lions off the animal.
Think of a neighbourhood watch that actually turns up,
where the cows weigh up to half a tonne and the bulls weigh more.

elements.text: COWS: UP TO HALF A TONNE.

shots.narration: Here's the part tourists filmed.
In September two thousand and four, at a watering hole in Kruger National Park,
tourists in a safari vehicle filmed lions catching a buffalo calf at the water's edge.
Then a crocodile came out of the water and tried to take the calf away from the lions.
Then the herd came back.
The buffalo surrounded the lions and drove them off one after another,
and the calf got free and walked back into the herd.
The video went online in two thousand and seven as Battle at Kruger,
and it has since been watched tens of millions of times.
Doug watched the whole thing from inside the vehicle, exactly like the people who filmed it.
Doug is fine.
For once, Doug stayed in the car.
The lions went home hungry, and for them this was a fairly normal day at work.
The Lion Killer.
For a lion, the buffalo is a favourite lunch,
and sometimes that lunch turns around and kills the lion.
In Kruger, a long-term study of hunting lions found that the males mainly caught buffalo.
But it is rarely a job for one lion,
since to bring down an adult buffalo, lions usually need a pride or a coalition of males working together.
The same study found that the size of the hunting group shaped both how often lions succeeded and what they chose to chase.
They also have to get close before anything starts.
A buffalo can outrun a lion by about ten kilometres an hour,
so lions have to ambush them from short range.
The ugly part is what happens next.
The buffalo does not run every time.
Lions that are too confident, or simply unlucky, have been killed by a buffalo's horns and its crushing weight.
Imagine a job where the main perk is a free lunch,
and the main workplace hazard is also the lunch.
Doug joined the pride as an intern, with a name badge.
Doug has worked with lions before,
and he did not learn anything then either.
The herd turned around.
The lions knew what that meant,
and Doug did not.
Doug deaths: four hundred and one,
and so far Doug has met one buffalo and one herd.
The dry season puts all of them in one place.
All of them.
The Megaherd.
In the dry season, buffalo herds merge at the last water into super-herds of a thousand or more.
As the pools dry up, herds that split apart during the rains converge on the rivers and waterholes that are left.
A group of a few dozen animals swells into hundreds,
and sometimes well over a thousand.
In Botswana's Mababe Depression, one guide looked across a single plain and estimated three thousand buffalo.
That is a crowd the size of a small town,
where every adult resident outweighs an upright piano.
Here's the problem.
A crowd that size does not stand still.
On a later drive, a visiting wildlife writer followed a dust cloud on the horizon
and found about five thousand buffalo moving together.
You may have heard that buffalo kill two hundred people every year,
but we could not find any published count behind that number.
What is documented is how a big herd treats lions.
Together, the herd can turn on the lions that are hunting it and send them running.
Doug is still wearing the lion badge.
A thousand buffalo arrived at the water and looked at the lion,
and then at the small man wearing its badge.
The lion ran,
and Doug did not.
Doug has died. Again.
When the dust settled, the herd was already leaving,
and the red cap was riding away on a buffalo's back among the oxpeckers.
It was the only part of Doug the herd agreed to keep.
Doug deaths: four hundred and two.
The number never goes down.
Subscribe, and watch where it goes up next.
